title: Most people think Gehazi’s problem was greed.
paragraphs: Most people think Gehazi’s problem was greed.
But the deeper warning in his story is what he was willing to run after.
Gehazi was not an outsider to God’s work.

He wasn’t a pagan.
He wasn’t an enemy of the prophet.
He was Elisha’s servant.
He had front-row seats to miracles.

He watched the sick healed.
He watched the impossible happen.
He watched the power of God move in ways most people in Israel would never see.
And then one day, a powerful man named Naaman arrived.
Naaman was a commander of the Syrian army, respected and feared—but he carried a disease that power could not fix.
Leprosy.
Through God’s mercy, Naaman followed the prophet’s instruction and washed in the Jordan River seven times.
And something incredible happened.
The disease left him.
His skin was restored like the skin of a child.
Imagine witnessing that moment.
A man who arrived broken… leaving healed.
Naturally, Naaman wanted to give gifts.

Silver.
Gold.
Fine garments.
But Elisha refused.
Not because wealth is evil.
But because this miracle needed to send a message louder than money:
God’s grace cannot be bought.
Naaman needed to return home knowing that the God of Israel heals by mercy—not by payment.
But Gehazi saw the moment differently.
While Elisha saw the glory of God, Gehazi saw a missed opportunity.
And one quiet thought entered his heart:
“Why should this man go away with all this?”
So Gehazi did something dangerous.
He ran.
He ran after Naaman’s caravan.
He invented a story.
He claimed that visitors had arrived and that his master now needed silver and garments.
Naaman gladly gave them.
And Gehazi hid the reward.
From the outside, it probably looked like a small victory.
He had gained wealth.
But the most chilling moment in the story happens when he returns to Elisha.
The prophet asks him one simple question:
“Where have you been, Gehazi?”
Not because Elisha lacked information.
But because God was exposing something deeper.
The running.
The secret.
The heart behind the decision.
Gehazi thought he was collecting treasure.
But he didn’t realize he was carrying something far heavier.
Elisha told him:
“Was not my spirit with you when the man got down from his chariot to meet you?”
Then came the judgment.
“The leprosy of Naaman shall cling to you and to your descendants forever.”
Think about the irony.
The disease that left Naaman fell on Gehazi.
The miracle moved forward.
The judgment moved backward.
Because there is a principle hidden in this story that many people overlook:
If you chase what God rejected, you may inherit what God removed.
Gehazi didn’t fall because he rejected God.
He fell because he chased something God had already said no to.
And that kind of temptation still exists today.
Not every opportunity is a blessing.
Some opportunities are tests of loyalty.
Some offers are disguised traps.
Some doors are open simply to reveal what is inside our hearts.
The most dangerous thing about Gehazi’s story is how familiar it feels.
Standing close to God’s work.
Seeing miracles.
Hearing truth.
But still allowing the heart to quietly run after something God never approved.
Because sometimes the biggest spiritual battles aren’t fought in public rebellion.
They happen in quiet decisions…
When no one else seems to be watching.
Except God.

Scripture:
2 Kings 5:20–27

Question for reflection:
What do you think is more dangerous: openly rejecting God, or quietly chasing something He already told you to leave alone?
